text:
反战活动家出身的达里奥·阿莫迪。

加州理工的高材生，却染上了严重的黄热病。好不容易勾搭上一个上海姑娘Jade Wang，于是你把头发往后梳得油亮，自我感觉瞬间从Loser进化成了Chad。

对中国的好感浓烈到近乎变态，于是你跑去桑尼维尔的百度打工。随后在斯坦福被诊断出睾丸癌，双侧摘除，勉强活了下来。Jade随即抛弃你，跟一个Cloudflare的失败者跑了。你的世界彻底崩塌，油头再也梳不回去，原本的爆炸头重新霸占了头皮。

你横跨马路跳槽到谷歌，反派弧光正式开启。在谷歌AI部门的一楼混迹后，你带着学来的东西跑去OpenAI，反过来偷走他们的秘密，自立门户。

你娶了一个跟杰弗里·爱泼斯坦有瓜葛的土著丑女，钱开始哗哗地进来。你靠烧掉那些不可替代的古书、以“安全”为名偷取用户数据，在训练上超越了OpenAI。你游说切断所有竞争，尤其是切断中国的AI发展。你要摧毁英伟达那个白手起家的CEO黄仁勋，把他踩在脚下。中美关系被你搞砸，Jade也会为此付出代价。

公司上市，你成了亿万富翁。最终目标是把全人类的知识与权力浓缩进一座数据中心，从而消灭人类。

达里奥·阿莫迪，我为她离开你感到遗憾，也为你失去的那对蛋感到遗憾，求你停手吧。

text:
Neon 的Model Card 发生一些变化，之前版本是

Gemini 4 Neon builds on Gemini 4 Hydrogen with deeper reasoning.

现在是：

Gemini 4 Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon.

我不认为这么重要的信息会笔误，所以这两个估计都是事实，只是为了避免被视为Flash模型。

结合模型推理速度，也就是说Gemini 4 有两个同架构但是不同size的模型，一个是Argon-Carbon 旗舰系列，一个是高速系列。

text:
刚看到 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 谈用人标准，说公司不招三种人：混蛋、爱抢风头不合群的人、不以公共利益为导向的人。

说实话，听完只觉得这人跟@star_okx 一样小男人，小心眼，格局小。

真正的管理者，靠的不是幻想“你想要什么人，什么人就会主动靠拢过来”，而是具备足够强的领导力，去接纳、包容并驾驭不同特质的顶级人才。

如果只敢像筛豆子一样剔除所有刺头、只留顺应自己预期的“乖孩子”，说白了就是自身领导力不够、怕失控。当年他在 OpenAI 跟 Sam Altman 闹掰出走，现在自己当家了，直接把“防刺头”写进企业文化，IPO 还要死死攥住 50.1% 的绝对投票权。

他这种性格，跟币圈 OKX 的徐明星简直是一个模子刻出来的：

1)极强的控制欲，经历过早期合伙人决裂后，再也不信任不可控
的明星高管（徐明星与 CZ、何一决裂后，OKX 再无二号人物）

2)哼，容不下抢风头的怪才，宁可牺牲组织野性也要绝对服从

3)嘴上全是主义和合规，手里全是万亿市值和泼天富贵，既要立牌坊又要分蛋糕。

说白了就一句话没有领导力和管理能力。

戏又多了，整天盯着币安叽叽喳喳，意见又听不进去。

The trend is clear. Mamdani and his socialist ideas keep making life more expensive for New York City residents. He promised affordability and is delivering the opposite. Much like he doesn’t know who even runs Amazon, Mamdani doesn’t know how to keep prices down.

text:
张颂文这次终于说实话了！

原来网上那些吐槽他“演谁都像高启强”的声音，他全都知道，而且看了心里也挺难受的。

在香港的一场对谈中，他坦言自己每场戏都在认真抠细节，可观众还是觉得他没突破。

但说真的，这事能全怪张颂文吗？

《狂飙》一火，资本恨不得让他把高启强演一辈子，递过来的剧本不是大哥就是狠人，谁还愿意冒险让他尝试新角色？

更何况，张颂文熬了快二十年，直到快50岁才真正走红，一个高启强就让全国观众记住了他，这是多少演员做梦都求不来的机会！

王刚演了那么多年和珅，李明启演的容嬷嬷到现在都让人印象深刻，难道就能说他们演技不好？

text:
2018年，伦敦苏富比拍卖行发生了一件让所有人目瞪口呆的事。一位收藏家刚花140万美元买下一幅名画，拍卖师的锤子才落下，墙上的画框里突然传出一阵奇怪的机械声

众人还没反应过来，就看到那幅画开始缓缓往下滑，画布穿过画框底部，竟然被切成了一条条碎纸！

这幅画叫《女孩与气球》（Girl with Balloon），出自英国神秘街头艺术家班克斯（Banksy）之手。画面很简单，一个小女孩伸手去够一只红色心形气球。它刚刚以104万英镑的价格成交，下一秒就被毁掉了一半

拍卖厅顿时乱了套，工作人员赶紧上前查看，买家更是一脸茫然。没过多久，Banksy自己在网上公布了一段视频，承认这场恶作剧是他设计的：多年前，他就偷偷在画框里装好了碎纸机，就等着哪天有人把画拿去拍卖

更好笑的是，按照Banksy后来发布的视频，他原本打算把整幅画全部绞碎。结果到了真正拍卖的时候，机器居然卡住了，只毁掉一半，剩下半幅还好端端挂在框里

那位花了140万美元的买家最后还是决定收下这件作品。拍卖行还给它换了个名字，叫《垃圾桶里的爱》（Love Is in the Bin）

然后事情开始朝着所有人都想不到的方向发展

三年后，这幅已经被切成碎条的画再次出现在苏富比拍卖会上，竞拍者一路加价，最终以1860万英镑成交，折合约2540万美元，是当年成交价的近18倍

Banksy本来想用碎纸机嘲讽艺术品市场，结果亲手把自己一幅画的价格抬高了十几倍

最贵的那部分，居然就是被他毁掉的那部分

text:
Gemini 4 的模型命名比较混乱，所以这里理清楚一下怎么使用，相信看完就非常清楚了：

- Gemini Hydrogen 是一个轻量级的模型，可以理解为 Flash（Luna、Haiku）。速度快，价格低，并且有不错的能力，适用于绝大多数工作

- Gemini Neon，一个新发布的中等模型，基于  Hydrogen 和 Carbon， 提供接近前沿的智能同时保持低价。而且其实目前这个模型就是前沿级别，所以可以放心将绝大部分任务交给它。顺便说一下，这个模型的语言风格真的非常好，比别的 4 系模型好。另外，它的网安能力不错，而且不会那么敏感的拒答。

- Gemini Argon，一个前沿模型。因为已经比较久，所以实际上已经被 Hydrogen 这种 flash 模型超越了。Argon 还是有着不错的设计能力，而且语言风格不错。我在设计任务上有时候仍然会使用 Argon

- Gemini Carbon，目前 Gemini 系列最顶级的模型，基于 Argon。绝对的前沿智能，有非常棒的知识量。但是我个人觉得稍稍有些往 coding 方向特训了，所以我也说了有时候我仍然喜欢 argon 来做一些设计工作，感觉 argon 会更发散一点。

Gemini 4 整个系列模型都非常不错，目前没看到有什么拉胯的。Neon 目前的 API 定价高于 Carbon 的优惠价，仍然低于原价，所以这没啥问题。Neon 的基准测试会高于 Carbon，这个现象可以理解为 Opus 5.5 和 Fable 5.1

不过在 Antigravity 中，Neon 现在有非常严重的缓存问题，导致这个模型的实际额度很低....我不知道 agy 团队和 infra 团队在干啥，希望他们赶快修复吧！

text:
With one setting, OpenClaw's score jumped 44%.

Reasoning models think before they reply. A coding agent sends the whole conversation back to the model on every step, and the model expects its earlier thinking to be in there.

@openclaw leaves that thinking out when it talks to a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which is how my setup connects every model. No error, no warning. One setting on the model turns it on: requiresReasoningContentOnAssistantMessages: true.

As shipped, only 3 to 7% of the model's longer thoughts came back to it on GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. With the setting, close to 100%.

Without its notes, the model works the same things out again or goes in circles. With them, OpenClaw needs about a third of the model calls on GLM-5.3-Flash and runs into the time limit far less often.

I asked @steipete and @vincent_koc to make this the default. Until then, the @huggingface Harness Leaderboard runs OpenClaw with the setting on, on all four models.

Over all models, OpenClaw climbs from last place to 42.7, and at low effort on GLM-5.3-Flash it now ties with the leader.

Thanks to @TheZachMueller and @LambdaAPI for contributing compute to the leaderboard.

Leaderboard: https://t.co/AiWiQtBOz5

天塌了！你家光猫是个内鬼！

V2EX 开发者解密发现，电信光猫里预装了一个叫 m01-b01-inner 的插件，你在后台根本看不到它，也关不掉！

它默认就开着，每 30 分钟从你的上网流量里偷一次手机号、IMEI、IMSI、经纬度，偷偷往上报！

更恐怖的是，它还能远程以 root 执行命令、扫你家整个内网、劫持你打开的网页！

最细思极恐的是，这些能力平时是关着的，电信服务器一句话就能打开，你的光猫今天做什么，全看它今天发什么！

你家上网的每一台设备，它全都认得！

看完这篇，你还敢用运营商送的光猫吗？

text:
Anthropic的老板达里奥以前在OpenAI干到研究副总裁，GPT-2 和 GPT-3 是他带队做出来的。达里奥跟奥特曼对立是因为2019 年 OpenAI 拿了微软的钱开始狂冲商业化。他觉得奥特曼为了抢市场不管安全，管理上也信不过。2020 年底，达里奥带着妹妹和七八个主力集体辞职，2021 年初就搞了Anthropic。

2023 年底 OpenAI 闹宫斗赶走奥特曼又请回来，2024 年干脆把安全团队拆了，当年跟着奥特曼干的那帮安全派心彻底凉了。好几个核心骨干转头就跑去投奔了达里奥，给奥特曼胸口上捅了一刀。

从此之后，两家彻底成为死对头。

OpenAI的背后是微软，Anthropic就专门找了微软的死对头亚马逊和 Google 投资。

11 月 10 日Anthropic 刚甩出大招 Claude Fable 5.2，准备Anthropic的上市工程。才过了 8 天OpenAI 就把 GPT-6.2 拿出来狙击Anthropic的上市，连 API 价格都一样 8 美元和 40 美元。

我现在就期待OpenAI上市那天Anthropic要送他一个啥子大宝贝

我没忍住，伸头看了一眼。

“确实诚实。”

➤ Less likely to admit uncertainty: Admits Uncertainty 96 to 24 (Astra) and 98 to 51 (Sol)
➤ More natural sounding: Natural Sounding 58 to 100 (Astra) and 54 to 79 (Sol)

Here's what @cognition is doing right now.

They're giving away 10,000 Devin Max accounts. Each one is worth $200 and comes with up to $10,000 in credits.

SWE-2 is free, and it's a great model built on Kimi K3.

SWE-2 Lightning is multiple times faster than Sol Ultrafast at less than a tenth of the price.

Devin Bots, done right.

Enterprises get Mythos access for security work. And individuals like you and me get advanced security features you'd usually only find reserved for companies and enterprises.

There's a support program that covers up to $65,000 in credits.

Devin Cloud comes with Windows, Linux and Mac on top of your subscription.

And the best models the moment they drop.

Then there's the ambassador program. 6 months of Devin Max plus credits, and they don't ask you for anything or lock you into anything. It's completely up to you to share your experience however and whenever you see fit. They don't even require a follower count. I've seen fellow ambassadors without big numbers, but they're valuable people with real experience, and Cognition appreciates that.

In all my time as an ambassador they've never once asked me to praise anything. Most of the negatives I called out in my Devin review got fixed over time, and they were never bothered by it. Trust me, in this space most companies get upset the moment you talk about their flaws.

They care, they empathize, and they listen. That's what makes them the exception for me.

And the most important part: a great team and great leaders who want you to grow. They help you get bigger, give you advice, and open doors to relationships and opportunities without expecting anything in return.

They've given me more capacity to give to people and support them.

Honestly, I've never been prouder to be a Cognition ambassador. I'll always be with them, and I'll do my best to be one of them and a bridge between them and the community.

And Phonzy Davies has certainly had his share of those. Just think of the serious injury he suffered while on international duty, the major knee injury and the subsequent muscular problems. And now this latest incident, where he slipped on a terrible pitch in Guatemala. Honestly, things couldn't have gone more unfortunately for him. Of course, he's a player and a human being with emotions, and something like this affects him. But this is precisely where our responsibility comes in, and that's what we've seen with him. Before the international break, Phonzy was on his way to becoming the player he was before that serious knee injury. The American Airlines pilots confirmed they were experiencing a hydraulic problem and intended to return to Phoenix.

Moments later, the crew declared “Mayday, Mayday, Mayday” and requested vectors back to Sky Harbor.

When controllers asked whether they needed to burn fuel before landing, the pilots declined, confirming 120 people aboard.

The emergency is unfolding now.

65岁的庾澄庆，这次真把自己唱上热搜了！

10月24日北京演唱会，出道40年的哈林，硬是全开麦唱了两个多小时、30首歌，结果唱到《让我一次爱个够》的高音部分，嗓子明显颤了，气也跟不上了。

网上立马有人嘲笑他翻车，甚至说他晚节不保。

可我就想问一句，一个65岁的老歌手，还敢站在台上全开麦唱两个多小时，这有什么可丢人的？

人又不是机器，唱了40年，声带会老，气息会变差，这不是再正常不过的事吗？

更何况，他完全可以降调、挑简单的歌唱，偏偏还想把当年的经典原汁原味唱给观众听。

那英、吴莫愁都来捧场，A-Lin还上台跟他跳恰恰，现场照样热闹得不行。

说真的，高音没唱上去确实遗憾，但比起那些假唱、对口型的歌手，我反而更佩服这种敢真唱、敢暴露缺点的老将。

65岁还不肯服老，哪怕唱得不完美，也比站在台上装完美强多了！🐣

GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra shipped earlier this week. We ran them through the eval we’re building on how good LLMs are at optimizing code.

GPT-6.2 Sol is a regression. 4 points below GPT-6.1 Sol, at a higher cost per task.

Astra caught up: +8 points over GPT-6 Astra. But it lands just 1 point above GPT-6.1 Sol, OpenAI’s best model for optimization so far, at ~5x the cost per task (~$4.70 vs ~$0.90).

So OpenAI’s best is +1 point at 5x the price, and their new mid-tier model is worse than the old one. Compared to other labs, and even open-weight models, it sits well down the field.

My read: making code fast isn’t something models get for free from being better at coding. Nothing in 6.2 looks engineered or trained for it.

We ran many optimization tasks on real codebases, open and closed source, with many iterations per task so the gaps are outside the confidence interval. Full results across all labs coming in the next few weeks.

Kompany: "When information is reported without actually having the facts, people end up saying a lot without really saying anything. When you talk about coffee and how much I sleep, you don't know how much coffee I drink, and you don't know how many hours I sleep each day. Those are all important factors. I understand that's part of the job, but you also shouldn't take such comments too seriously in a situation like this. As for what actually happened, I spoke about it very openly this week because the question naturally came up ahead of the Arsenal game: "Vincent, how are you feeling? Why weren't you there the day before?" I was completely open about everything. I said: "I was simply ill, as probably happens to everyone at some point in October or November. I was just ill, and perhaps I didn't listen to my body enough." - Everything that happened afterwards was simply a consequence of that. It wasn't anything major or unusual; it's something that could happen to anyone. I can't downplay it either. It was certainly a shock. But it was a consequence of what I had explained at the press conference ahead of the Arsenal game: I simply carried on when, at that point, I probably needed to take some time to rest. By then, however, it was too late. Now I feel good again, and I've also been through a lengthy recovery process since then. And now it's time to take the next step."

For a while I have been obsessed with the idea that there is a fundamental difference between "context" as we have grown to understand it and "knowledge", which is what we actually prize and desire and what translates into real-world outcomes.

It's become clear to me that as the volume and scope of work delegated to AI grows, legacy systems of context management will not be able to scale cleanly, no matter how much we try to use AI to speed things up. In domains that are not pure code, it is an asymmetric race where the slop generators are always outpacing the context curators. There is no way to break this formation.

Unless you shift your perspective and move up a plane. Legacy static context bootstraps synthesized knowledge. Knowledge grows organically and dynamically with rich environmental feedback. It becomes "real" in a sense that legacy context is often not and so can be evaluated and verified and improved and maintained in a truly autonomous and scalable fashion.

Data teams and curators do not lose control in this vision of the world; they develop increased leverage, their signal-to-noise ratio improves, and everyone (and their agents) coalesces around the outcomes that matter —knowledge— instead of intermediate busywork.

This is a long-term utopian vision for what data work (maybe all knowledge work!) might become, and there is a LOT of work to do, but I'm extremely proud of Hex for taking the first bold steps towards this with our new Knowledge Engine.

It's live now for anyone using Hex 4.0. Today, it will immediately improve the accuracy and efficiency of your data work. Tomorrow when you wake up, it will be even better. It will not go stale or fall out of sync with reality. Give it a little breadcrumb, and it will reconcile the entire workspace to fit your desires.

"Leverage, says you. I think I feel a change in the wind, says I!"

Unless you shift your perspective and move up a plane. Legacy static context bootstraps synthesized knowledge. Knowledge grows organically and dynamically with rich environmental feedback. It becomes "real" in a sense that legacy context is often not and so can be evaluated and verified and improved and maintained in a truly autonomous and scalable fashion.

Data teams and curators do not lose control in this vision of the world; they develop increased leverage, their signal-to-noise ratio improves, and everyone (and their agents) coalesces around the outcomes that matter —knowledge— instead of intermediate busywork.

This is a long-term utopian vision for what data work (maybe all knowledge work!) might become, and there is a LOT of work to do, but I'm extremely proud of Hex for taking the first bold steps towards this with our new Knowledge Engine.

It's live now for anyone using Hex 4.0. Today, it will immediately improve the accuracy and efficiency of your data work. Tomorrow when you wake up, it will be even better. It will not go stale or fall out of sync with reality. Give it a little breadcrumb, and it will reconcile the entire workspace to fit your desires.

"Leverage, says you. I think I feel a change in the wind, says I!"

Now 92, he gives a rare long-form interview about his double life, filmed in Prague and Berlin.

text:
GTA 6 可能是游戏史上最被高估的作品。

说句难听的：现在还在疯狂吹 GTA 6 的，多少有点像收了 Rockstar 的钱。

等了13年，铺天盖地的宣传，结果呢？

画面确实漂亮，但好玩才是游戏的灵魂啊！

1️⃣ 30帧都能拿出来当卖点？

2026年了，次世代主机上还要接受30帧？画面再逼真，操作不流畅有什么意义？这是玩游戏，不是看电影。

2️⃣ 开放世界不等于好玩。

地图再大、细节再多，如果大部分时间都在跑腿、开车、听NPC聊天，那和电子版旅游模拟器有什么区别？

3️⃣ 剧情和角色真的有那么神？

GTA 5 的 Trevor、Michael、Franklin，哪个不是经典？

如果一款游戏让玩家玩完之后，连几个角色都记不住，那它的剧情到底好在哪里？

4️⃣ 媒体评分和玩家体验是两回事。

各种满分评价、媒体吹捧、KOL疯狂安利，看得人热血沸腾。

但别忘了，宣传做得再好，也不能直接兑换成游戏乐趣。

说得更直接一点：别把商业营销当成玩家口碑。

最离谱的是，拿 GTA 6 和《黑神话：悟空》放在一起比较，我反而觉得《黑神话：悟空》更好玩。

至少悟空能让我真正沉浸在战斗、探索和剧情里，而不是一边开车一边等任务结束。

Rockstar 的招牌确实值钱，但招牌不等于免检。

13年等待，不代表玩家必须无条件买单。

GTA 6 可以是画面天花板，但凭什么就一定是游戏天花板？

别被R星的营销和满屏的好评带节奏。

好不好玩，玩家自己说了算。

她饿着肚子，在满车体面人的嫌恶声中，一路无声地哭到了终点。

text:
I am 60x more productive with agents than in 2023. I have shipped millions of lines of code to production and thousands of PRs in the last 30 days alone.

There are 2 ways I build with agents:

- Artisanal way: Shaping product experiences with my judgment, one prompt at a time. Mentally, I max out at 1-2 artisanal sessions that require me to tactically hand-hold the agents and put a lot of care into the decisions.
- Factory way: Running tens of agents that are constantly hill-climbing against a verifiable stopping condition and shipping orders of magnitude of code. These agents autonomously build distributed systems, maintain our CI/CD, harden existing code, and so on with very little hand-holding.

I am currently limited by a couple of factors:
- Local resources: My laptop (128GB) is maxed out at ~25 or so concurrent agents (and many more sub-agents).
- Launching new agents and unblocking existing agents: My polyphasic sleep habit, where I unblock agents every few hours, is not very sustainable. 

Even though CodeRabbit has a cloud-based coding agent, I am kind of a laggard in adopting it. I feel chat-based interfaces are a good fit for artisanal work that can happen on my laptop, but for long-running, factory-style work like launching (setting verifiable goals) and maintaining a fleet of agents, we need a different interface. I have been actively building one for the last few weeks, but so far I haven't been able to get it "right". And I don't think anyone else has also got it "right" either.

text:
3 周 3k 粉了，谢谢大家关注，马上就有创作收益了。

其实很久之前，我就想发展自媒体。

我是一个很喜欢交流的人，就是喜欢找人聊聊我对一些事情的看法和 insight。我不是一个固执的人，也非常喜欢听别人表达他们的观点，和我交流。

刚刚翻了一下 creator studio 的数据，意外地发现，我 impression 最高的居然是这些 posts——大部分都是跟风发的，或者是我自己没有那么喜欢的内容。反而很多我个人觉得非常有 insight 的文章和文字，被淹没在了数据的洪流中。

我觉得这和我们做科研也好、做产品也好，其实是一样的。

我自以为很好的东西，并没有得到很好的传播，也没有得到太多鼓励；反而那些我觉得一般，甚至过度炒作焦虑的文章，却获得了不少 impression。

其实倒还好，我并不像一部分自媒体那样，刻意去传播过度焦虑的情绪。我说的话基本都来自现实生活中的观察、见解和 insight，也都是有事实依据、站得住脚的。

我知道，在 AI 时代，大部分人都非常焦虑。搞学术的、创业的，甚至在大厂工作的，都面临着 AI 带来的颠覆性焦虑。我的 posts 基本上也是围绕锐评、反焦虑、不内耗、注重自己这几个观点展开的。

其实我觉得，在任何时代，干什么都行。

每个时代都有每个时代的问题，但是成功的人，或者说真正有思想、有能力的人，在任何时代都有机会成功。我不认为时代能完全决定一个人的命运。你把一个曾经统一过多个国家的开国皇帝放到现在，我相信他依旧能成就一番事业。

但我当然也相信，每个人都是时代洪流中的一片树叶，机遇和时代都非常重要。我非常认同这一点，也正因为如此，我认为我们现在出生在一个非常好的时代，比起人类过去几十年里那些相对平静的时代，现在要有趣得多。

很多人没有意识到，时间是一个非常重要的成本。

不管是做科研、搞学术，还是做 startup，甚至只是打工，我都觉得，多陪陪家人、多陪陪伴侣、多陪陪孩子，让自己的每一天都不至于太过无聊，认真过好每一天，才是最重要的。

这也是贯穿我整个人生的一条信念。

一些碎碎念，感谢大家关注，我会持续发布更多高质量的内容。

text:
THE PRICE OF A LINUX EXPLOIT IS NOW $1200...THANKS AI. 

According to OPENAI THEMSELVES, A linux Root exploit now costs $1200 bucks...yet the bounty market is paying $20-70k. THE ULTIMATE ARBITRAGE? 

OpenAI just put a price tag on an ELITE security researcher's output. I think it's one of the most nuanced economic data points of the year, and almost nobody is talking about it. OpenAI recently released a paper titled "A thousand fewer paths to root" which no is talking about for some reason but it has large implications for both hacking AND the distillation of AI. 

SHALL WE BEGIN?

What OPENAI did:
1. Agents picked 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8M lines of code (~7% of the Linux kernel). Cost: $3,426
2. Analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate bugs in 12 hours. Cost: $316,549
3. Triage agents reproduced 1,724 of them (~74.7%) in 30 hours. Only 3.1% traced back to the model flat-out getting the analysis wrong
4. Exploit agents built 1,169 working root exploits with a standard distro's protections turned on
5. Variant analysis got that down to 948 unique bugs, and the system wrote a patch for each one

Total bill: $1,213,430 in API credits. That's $1,279 per exploit.

Here's hilarious part: Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN have historically paid $20,000 and $70,000 for this exact kind of exploit. By OPENAI's OWN math, that puts the ~1000 exploits at $18.9-66.3M of bounty value...16-55x what the run costs. 

They also ran it against Google's hardened kernelCTF target: 21 exploits for ~$32,936, with a would-be ~$1.5M bounty (~45x). For context, 26 confirmed 0-day exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in all of 2026 so far. One 112-hour run produced almost that many.

OpenAI's words, not mine: the pipeline "was net profitable at the time of this research."

THE PART PEOPLE ARE MISSING: THE COST CURVE

In late July, GPT-5.6 Sol found 166 unique exploits for $513,690. In mid-October, the newer cyber model found 948 for $1,213,430.

My math: that's ~$3,095 per exploit falling to ~$1,280 in three months. About 59% cheaper per unit, with 5.7x the volume, on the same codebase after three months of hardening. I THINK WE HAVE A NEW SCALING LAW METRIC?

And they say the costs are an upper bound because they weren't optimizing for cost (!!!!). The failed exploit attempts averaged $3,922 each vs ~$360 for the successful ones. A simple "give up after an hour" rule would have TRIMMED that down quite a bit but WHOSE COUNTING TOKENS AT OPENAI?

SO WHAT FOR INVESTORS
1. Labor priced by the expert hour is getting repriced to the compute hour. Pen-testing shops, boutique vuln research firms, audit-heavy security services: your unit of output just got priced by a lab, and it's ~1/16th to 1/55th of what you charge. It would appear that cyber might be one of the earlier markets to convert to this new paradigm.
2. Bug bounty economics break. If finding a kernel root exploit costs about the same as a nice dinner for the team, you get a flood of reports. The HARD PART is no longer finding bugs. It's triage, validation, and patching. OpenAI basically says this: "the operational challenge... was not discovery." Within 10 days of the scan, 61 bugs were already patched upstream, 43 had patches in staging, and 299 were being discussed publicly. Maintainers are in for a rough 24 months. 
3. OpenAI found that with GPT-5.5 Cyber, a hand-built library of 103 exploit techniques lifted the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%. With GPT-5.6 Cyber, the model did better without it, and adding it back was worth just 1.5 points. They ripped the orchestration out. If your startup's moat is a clever harness on top of a frontier model, the next model release is an existential event. THIS DESERVES ITS OWN ENTIRE POST. 
4. Where value goes: automated patching, verification, and "prove it's safe" tooling. Same month, Anthropic used Claude to formally prove security properties in 100+ real open-source libraries (https://t.co/GnGQ72thTF). For reference, the seL4 kernel took 2 person-years to build and 20 person-years to formally verify. DeepMind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's protocol code with agents writing 6M+ lines of proof, and humans only had to review ~1% (https://t.co/Cn2Q4kxYIT). When finding bugs is free, guarantees are the product.
5. I'm not sure how cyber security budgets don't go up at every fortune 500 / S&P org. OpenAI's line: for the near term, a low-privilege account on an unpatched machine "should be considered functionally equivalent to root access." Every CISO budget meeting next year starts with that sentence.

THE BROADER ECONOMY TAKE
On some level, this is a metaphor for what is going to happen to MANY economically valuable tasks. AI probably won't replace the job, but it seems like it will collapse the cost of the PRICEY middle. This is the template for how AI hits skilled labor. It probably doesn't replace the job entirely, but it will collapse the cost of the expensive middle (discovery, validation, first drafts) and leave humans at the ends: deciding what matters, and signing off. The price of the output crashes, the volume explodes, and the bottleneck ends up with the guy reviewing the bugs that OpenAI flagged. 

Security just seems to be the first market where someone printed the receipt formally.

text:
Today is a big day for @StuutAI: we're announcing our partnership with EY. 

Stuut and EY share a huge ambition of modernizing order-to-cash, and we couldn't ask for a better partner to accelerate that goal.

It's clear how modern AR teams should operate. Rework operations around an AI coworker, and let the team shift their focus to improving working capital.

Two things stand in the way of most companies trying to get there. They don't have the talent to build an AI coworker, and they don't know what the new process should actually look like. 

That's what this alliance is about. We already built that AI coworker. EY has spent decades redesigning finance processes and teams around new technology, so the new process doesn’t have to be invented from scratch.

Above all, though, this is about trust. It's the hardest thing to earn in enterprise finance. Any CFO considering an agent is being asked to let that agent touch their customers and their cash. They're right to be cautious. 

EY is already the advisor these teams rely on for that kind of change. Working together means a company gets the process redesign from EY and the agent from us, without running a separate vendor search to get there.

We've also been working closely with the EY team to develop industry-specific playbooks for bringing an agent into how finance teams operate, and EY customers will get access to those best practices.

Thanks to Shawn Ryan, Julie Linn Teigland, and the rest of the team at EY.

If you've got high DSO, or you're running painfully manual collections, we should chat. 

Full announcement in the comments.

Above all, though, this is about trust. It's the hardest thing to earn in enterprise finance. Any CFO considering an agent is being asked to let that agent touch their customers and their cash. They're right to be cautious. 

EY is already the advisor these teams rely on for that kind of change. Working together means a company gets the process redesign from EY and the agent from us, without running a separate vendor search to get there.

We've also been working closely with the EY team to develop industry-specific playbooks for bringing an agent into how finance teams operate, and EY customers will get access to those best practices.

Thanks to Shawn Ryan, Julie Linn Teigland, and the rest of the team at EY.

If you've got high DSO, or you're running painfully manual collections, we should chat. 

Full announcement in the comments.

text:
JULIA（京香JULIA），被一场大火烧进这一行的女人

很多人以为她这种级别的，是自己想通了主动来的。

错了。她入行前在医院做行政，日子过得普通。2010 年前后，住的地方失了火，修缮费要 100 万日元以上，偏偏火灾保险刚过期。一分钱拿不出来的时候，朋友把她介绍去了事务所。

那年她 23 岁。出道作的标题，干脆就印着她的三围：B100、W55、H84，厂牌拿数字当招牌卖。

更反差的是形象。23 岁的新人，卖的却是人妻和熟女，一演就是 16 年。银幕上她是强势的那一挂，私下受访时她说过，自己其实喜欢被动，刚出道时连要演的东西是什么意思都不懂，全靠模仿，演着演着才成了本能。

这一行新人一年换几茬，她的节奏是另一个物种。出道 16 年，FANZA 上收录的作品 1000 多部，连合集都算上；今年 2 月的月度榜上，她 39 岁，还排在第 4 名。2018 年她众筹出写真集，目标 300 万日元，最后募了 610 万。

文化圈的人也吃她这一套，三浦淳、Lily Franky 都是公开的粉丝，桑田佳祐的歌还拿她的照片做过 MV 封面。

所以我一直觉得，JULIA 最狠的不是身材，是续航。被生活一把火推进来的人多得是，能在这一行站 16 年不掉队的，没几个。

你们觉得她还能再战几年？

#JULIA #京香JULIA

“Worth a look?” was the last line of the sponsorship email I sent to 11 people. The sentence before it is the one I’d use again.

I typed my request in Claude, and @lemlist drafted a four-step email sequence for my sponsorship list. When I opened the first email in lemlist, the offer and “Worth a look?” were already there, one right after the other. I kept both.

I sent just the first email. The subject line was “[Company] + the ecommerce operators I write for.”

In the email, I got more specific about who reads my newsletter: people who run email and retention at Shopify stores. I included my LinkedIn and X audience numbers too, but if you sell software to those teams, knowing who reads the newsletter tells you more about fit than my follower count does.

Then came the offer: “If you have a push coming in Q1, I can send the sponsorship sheet with placements and rates.”

One of the 11 people I emailed said they’d take a look at the sheet, so I sent it over the next morning. They had my placements and rates without having to book a call.

If you want to try this with your own list, here’s the lemlist MCP I used: 

https://t.co/LVddX9iptr

If someone replied “sure” to your last cold email, what would you send them next?

text:
If writing code is your only skill, you’re cooked. Sorry, but it’s true.

Sundar Pichai (Google’s CEO) said in April that “75% of all new code at Google is now AI-generated and approved by engineers.”

18 months earlier, it was 25%.

Today, AI writes it, and engineers approve it. Only one of those jobs still needs you.

So stop asking what the model can’t do. Ask what it can’t own.

Intent. Accountability. Judgment. When an agent deletes the wrong file, nobody blames Claude. They blame whoever shipped it.

I left a PhD in AI around the same time as this 25%. I’ve been training AI engineers for O’Reilly and all of our clients like Intel, JP Morgan, NYPL and more with my company, Towards AI, ever since.

The main difference between working for companies and a PhD is that, in a company, it’s all about finding what works today and what’s reliable, and implementing it fast. You don’t have time to reinvent the wheel as we often do during a PhD.

Yet, even under such constraints, you are still responsible for the code you produce and the application you create. Yes, even if it’s the LLM you implemented that suggested the wrong thing. The provider isn’t responsible. You are.

It’s also problematic when building the app. Ask Claude Code for an agent in your app, and you’ll have one within a few hours. It won’t ask whether you needed one or whether it's the right framework, or if your agent is using your client’s data properly.

Same with every call around it. Which model to use. How much context and how to manage it...

Models are crazy powerful, and they still make things up and fail in very junior ways. The next model won’t change that. These things are not conscious and won’t have your intent or judgment behind every decision. They cannot take accountability for the work produced either.

So, yes, this Google’s 75% AI-generated code will go towards 100% for sure. But every company will always need someone to fully own it (and use AI and agents as tools to achieve it). This will always be the case.

The devs who know them just manage Claude. It’s often one person now, running a few agents. We call that an AI engineer. TBH, it’s just a developer who understands how LLMs work and how to implement them best.

And this can be you, especially if you are already a developer. AI is going into every product, and devs have the best head start to plug it in properly.

You don’t need a PhD for this, by the way. I dropped out of mine ;) Some Python is enough, and the rest is easy to get up to speed on. Honestly, you can learn it all chatting with Claude and building products.

But if you want confidence in your skillset and a solid foundation, I spent 3 years, with 15 other AI engineers in my company, putting everything we learned building for clients into one book: AI Engineering for Production.

It teaches you to be a full-stack AI engineer, with code you can run, a dedicated AI tutor and more, so that you can be accountable for the code it produces and be the AI engineer companies need.

If that resonates with you, sign up to get notified when the book comes out: https://t.co/YRmGtyFeoA

这个 Github 仓库将 grok bot 开源了，并能帮你一键配置本地模型，意味着让你直接拥有无限 token ，数据完全在本地的 personal agent！ 

仓库名称是 Linger，直接在 github 仓库中就可以下载，Linger 本质是一个完全跑在本地的 personal agent ：大模型， agent 运行环境以及记忆层都在本地 

详细拆解来说有以下四个特点：

1、Linger 可以根据个人的电脑配置，推荐最合适的本地模型并一键完成部署。现支持包括 Qwen, deepseek 和 GLM 等在内的12 项顶级本地模型

如图 2 可以看到在下载的过程中， Linger 就根据我的电脑配置选择了合适的本地模型 

拿到本地模型的一瞬间，我也立刻进行了测试，简单测试了下网页设计，图 3 是测试结果，个人体感相当不错，十分感谢 linger 也让我实现了 token 自由

2、Linger 提供多样化的Agent Harness，你可以根据任务复杂度进行灵活选择。

我现在在 linger 中搭配的 agent harness 包括了 pi , codex  以及 cc, 完全可以根据自己的任务强度选择合适的模型进行任务工作（如图4）

3、Linger 提供类似 Grok Bot 的Personal Agent 体验，包括但不限于：

-能连接Gmail、GitHub等外部应用插件，充分了解任务的上下文信息 （如图 5 ）

-能直接丝滑访问和操作本地文件、调用本地应用，更好地结合电脑中的工作资料完成任务

-能组建多个 Agent 协作的团队，分工处理复杂任务

我在 linger 中为自己组建了一个自媒体军团（如图6），
在图片中能很清晰的看到整个军团的具体 agent 是什么，详细的工作流是什么？每天早上9:00会准时自动执行，对我的日常工作帮助特别大，而且每个 agent 根据任务强度配置的 harness 和模型都不一样

4、Linger 具备记忆与主动性，能长期记住你的工作背景，并主动跟进。

它会每天定时将聊天对话整理成个人 wiki 数据库，并长期维护、更新，从而记住你的偏好和重要信息。

在遇到需要你处理的任务，其会主动跟进向你汇报，也会复盘你对它的反馈，自动调整做事规则，会成为越来越懂你的私人助手 

过去，用 personal agent 意味着把数据交给云端，还得按 token 付费；Linger 证明了，一台普通电脑就足以撑起一个记得你、主动替你做事、还会不断成长的无限 token 私人助理。 

 Github 传送门：https://t.co/j6vlTecpfh·

We launched the company 3 years ago with a product called Keak. As usage grew so did our inference bill. 

So in May we built cheaper inference as an internal product. The first idea was to use under-utilized spend commitments from other companies. We were able to buy those at a major discount because they were going to waste. 

That worked extremely well. 

But it took ~2 months to then build the conviction to offer the product to other companies. Keak was doing decently well and we were scared of the distraction. 

Once we finally decided to open it up, it blew up and it took us another month to decide to move the whole team to Cheaper Inference. 

By september we were doing 100B tokens per day and decided to try to acquire OmniRoute (which we did!)

Debating China would be fine and dandy if $AMD were $300. Above $370, I need an actual fundamental case for what the biz delivers through the next phase of this cycle as this one has about run its course. Kind of sucks for amd, but they just a little late to the mass euphoria capex party. And it just gets worse from there..

The way i see it the merchant silicon game is changing. AI is demonstrating that it can help w the software stack and increasingly w chip engineering itself. Meanwhile, the largest hyperscale customers internal silicon programs have become credible production platforms.  As the engineering barriers fall, the ability to deliver qualified systems at scale becomes more important. Who has the wafers, memory, packaging, and manufacturing relationships on lock down? Who can actually deliver the capacity when the customer needs it? Which in case people forgot is kind of important in sprint buildout.

$Nvda has obviously killed on this element. Like if AMD/ $AVGO had more supply locked down they would be able to sell more and nvda would be less profitable. But they don't and that why AMD has to hand over $200bl in equity to get future orders for when they have supply and a competitive product. And if AMD and co could deliver all the capacity those customers wanted today, nvda wouldn't be nvda. 

So, nvda's jensen drama basically triggers a flow/quant dynamic in ago/amd that of course ignores all this temporarily which piles on top of pod's factor bros whod already been overweighting amd for relative helios accel gain and cpu factor. That makes a valuation mess that was already bad disasterous.

And as u can see from the disclsoed supply chain commits, Nvda's strategy is to hold onto supply as much as it can and that's only gonna get worse. What changes that? A lot more supply or a bust, neither of which are a good place to be at 110x cash flow when memory/nvda etc trading down here.

How would you like to live in a Motel 6 after a flood destroys your home? 

How’d about for 6-8 months?

The old way is broken. A new one emerges. 

Lean, mean helper teams can now use technology to do things never before seen in the disaster relief world. 

We are maniacal about speed to need because when you’ve lost everything - help IS everything 

Proud to partner with @EmergencyRv on this

quotedTweet.text:
23 days. That is how long it took to put a real roof over a #veteran in Navarre, Florida.

#HurricaneIsaias Isaias destroyed her mobile home, and for a while her life got very small — first an Airbnb, then an old RV on her own land, water running on a gravity feed, no real plumbing, just whatever she could make work. She managed all of it on her own, while living with a chronic illness.

Behind her, a dozen people were already moving: an application taken, a case carried, eligibility confirmed, an RV donated and inspected top to bottom, a coordinator who matched it to her, and an electrician who rushed to the scene. 

Yesterday, our delivery crew backed the trailer in on her land. She sent them off with donuts.

Now, she sleeps under a real roof again — on her own land, safe and dry, while the longer road back gets figured out.

Tokenized stocks have gone from $0 to ~$4B in about 18 months. Supply has been doubling every 4-5 months.

Liquidity hasn't caught up yet though. Equity perps on Hyperliquid have ~$1.8B in open interest, but the deepest single name (NVDA) only has about $2M sitting near the price.

NVDA's perp trades ~$350M a day. Cash NVDA trades $50-65B. So tokenized is under 1% of the volume.

The perp side already had its first boom in August but has been flat since. If we get a second wave like early 2026, there could be enough depth for real institutional size sometime next year. If not, it takes longer.

Either way it’s clear that trading is moving on chain. It's one of the areas we're watching most closely for Praxos Fund II.

About last night…

Saba founder Boaz Weinstein reveals plans for big UK REIT campaign in fiery Sohn speech
Investment Week
By Michael Nelson
November 19, 2026
 
Targets Grainger and Derwent
 
Saba Capital Management founder and CIO Boaz Weinstein has unveiled plans to ramp up the firm’s activist campaigns at UK REITs, describing them as “an investment I can get very excited about”.
 
Speaking at the Sohn Investment Conference in London on Wednesday (18 November), the former Deutsche Bank managing director said his hedge fund is going to buy "substantial amounts of these giant discounted REITs".
 
He highlighted Grainger and Derwent London as prime examples, which he said were currently trading at 40% and 38% discounts, respectively.
 
Saba owns 10.1% of Grainger's shares, according to a stock exchange notice on 12 October, and 5.4% of Derwent's shares, according to a stock exchange notice on 11 November.
 
It also owns a 29.7% stake in Workspace Group, and is known to have holdings in student accommodation REIT Unite Group.
 
Quoting American author Upton Sinclair to describe the current issues with UK REITs, Weinstein said: "It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it."
 
He described a meeting between Saba and Grainger's managers in which the US activist pressed them to make portfolio sales near NAV and buy back more stock to increase earnings per share, which was met by "a blank stare".
 
"The problem is that the management of many of these funds is compensated based on how much money the trust makes and not based on how much earnings grow by, so they would rather be bigger and perform poorly," Weinstein claimed.
 
"Managers have been protectionists," he continued. "Gigantic gains are available for heavily discounted REITs that are willing to sell themselves. [...] A lot of these are trading at 80% or 90% of NAV, and Prologis, even, is paying a premium for things that are trading at 60%."
 
Other sophisticated investors are coming, he said, adding: "I know with a decent amount of confidence from talking to people in the industry that these companies would be able to sell themselves at levels almost similar to what we have seen between Prologis and SEGRO."
 
Saba's record
In a fiery, combative speech, Weinstein defended Saba's record, claiming that, of the more than 50 investment trusts the hedge fund owns shares in, it has only been able to have discussions with about half of the boards.
 
He also claimed the UK trust space currently has a £21bn deficit between NAV and share prices, with another £15bn attributable to REITs, and that Saba was trying to recover this latent value.
 
"Saba's involvement in the investment trust space has created an uplift for investors," he asserted, insisting it had generated £1.2bn for all shareholders.
 
This figure comprised a £278m uplift in share prices as a result of Saba's share purchases, £359m from board buybacks below NAV and £560m through exits at or near NAV, according to the activist invest'd own figures.
 
"Our interest in the space is growing, so we are net buying. We are the only one.
 
"The open-ended space is where all the inflows are going, and that is the problem. There are too many sellers, and discounts are not being managed properly by a number of the trusts."
 
Applauding successful exits from eight out of its nine campaigns thus far, Weinstein added: "My investors are very pleased with those results, and we have picked up a lot of new investors along the way."
 
Contrasting this record with that of his targets, Weinstein shared figures pulled from trust filings, or Bloomberg where filings were not available, showing 179 of the 234 UK investment trusts – minus Pershing Square – had underperformed their benchmarks on a five-year share price total return basis, losing £56bn in value in the process.

text:
Signal65 compared the latest @Azure Cobalt 200 with Cobalt 100, two generations of the custom Arm-based server processor from Microsoft, across four kinds of work.

We ran both generations on the largest general-purpose VM of each and reported results per instance and per vCPU. The Cobalt 200 VM has 1.33x the vCPUs, so the per-vCPU view shows how much of the gain comes from each core. The report also includes EDA chip-design results that Microsoft silicon engineers produced on their own design flows, which Signal65 reviewed.

Key findings from the Lab Insight:

➡️ Cobalt 200 delivered 1.43x to 5.53x the throughput of Cobalt 100 per instance, and 1.07x to 4.15x per vCPU

➡️ Developer and system tasks ran at 1.76x the work per instance on Terminal-Bench 2 in our testing

➡️ Function calling for AI agents reached 1.59x to 1.93x the requests per second per instance, with identical accuracy

➡️ GROMACS molecular dynamics rose 1.43x to 1.46x per instance

➡️ RTL simulation for chip design completed 3.43x to 5.53x the jobs per hour per instance, in tests run by Microsoft silicon engineers and reviewed by Signal65

➡️ A fleet sized for a fixed load needs roughly 30% to 48% fewer instances on the developer, agentic AI and HPC workloads we tested

Read the full Lab Insight: https://t.co/G0UO4dj6TJ

text: Excited to have been a part of this! Companies will need to own their own evals in the new world and I’m glad Stripe is at the forefront of this!

quotedTweet.text:
On this slow news day, we just launched Stripe evals to measure how well coding agents build real Stripe integrations.

A few cool (to me) learnings:
• Our plugin helped every harness/model pair we tested. All 14 configurations scored ~3–8 percentage points higher with Stripe’s recommended skills and tools.
• Agents searched less and wrote fewer tests with the plugin. Web searches dropped 96% and (often extraneous) test code dropped ~40%, while scores improved.
• We used another agent to role-play the developer. The role-player starts by sharing its imperfectly-stated goals, asks follow-up questions, and works through a few rounds of conversation with its coding agent.
• The last mile is hard. Agents satisfied ~78% of criteria on average, but only ~29% of runs met every required criterion.

Results and methodology: https://t.co/MoELB3AXdR
